commenti.body: That's a very good analysis.  What's your take on the CIA's position? At the end, the CIA pretty much didn't care what happened as long as it didnt make a mess for them.  I thought that was brilliant. The characters were all main characters in their CIA caper and the CIA couldn't care less.  The CIA didnt want change.  As long as the status quo was not interrupted then why turn over rocks?

I think the CIA at the end is like the universe, they go, ok nothing breaks our rules, a bunch of stuff happened. Let it be. I don’t know why this happened or what we learned but it’s a go on our end, everything’s in order in its random disordered state.

I think you're right to call this something vaguely cosmic because it's a nihilism movie, it's a sequence of people attempting to create meaning out of something meaningless (the disk). If the CIA is a sort of personification of the universe, it makes sense it would be flummoxed by a human attempt to rationalize its motions. 

I suppose in light of this I'd read the men in cars aspect a little different. Now I haven't seen the film in a bit so I could be off here, but isn't the only confirmed man in car the lawyer or whatever at the end? If so, this feels to me like another aspect of putting too much weight on a random event. George Clooney thinks people are out to get him, and I guess technically he's right, but it's not the conspiracy he thinks it is. He's just trying to form greater meaning out of more nothingness.

I appreciate that you posted this long and thoughtful analysis of a film I just revisited this last week.  I have no criticism of your points.  I wonder if the desire for change/transformation which motivates so much of the action might not have something to do with almost all the characters being middle-aged?  For what it is worth, I've always regarded this as a rather minor film from major filmmakers.  I vaguely recall that when it was released many critics felt that there were too many 'morons' running around for one movie.
